extracted.intended_audience: literate readers, essayists, playwrights, actors, and theatre-goers interested in taste, wit, and public manners (early-18th-century audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice and standards for producing and judging wit, theatrical taste, and public decorum as given in Spectator essays; covers forms of humor (punning, biting), acceptable stage content, audience behaviour, and related social prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory as a valued literary form
rubrics_metrics.description: As some of the finest Compositions among the Ancients are in Allegory, I have endeavoured ... to revive that way of Writing, and hope I have not been altogether unsuccessful in it; for I find there is always a great Demand for those particular Papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegory is presented as a respected classical mode worth reviving; it is useful for moral instruction and is in demand. (Context: the editor introduces a Vision written in allegory as appropriate for treating serious passions like grief.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Good theatrical taste prefers sober, polite mirth to coarse laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: I drew this Morning Conclusions ... from the reading a Comedy of Terence. The Play was the Self-Tormentor. It is from the Beginning to the End a perfect Picture of human Life, but I did not observe in the whole one Passage that could raise a Laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refined audiences appreciate subtle, humane sentiments rather than broad or grotesque comic effects. The author contrasts Terence's restrained comedy (which pleases polite minds) with contemporary stage entertainments that provoke coarse mirth; implication: writers/actors should aim for natural, humane depiction rather than gross spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage portrayals that provoke laughter from pain or indecency are signs of bad taste
rubrics_metrics.description: According to what you may observe there on our Stage, you see them often moved so directly against all common Sense and Humanity, that you would be apt to pronounce us a Nation of Savages... an old Woman carried off with a Pain in her Side ... was laughed and clapped off the Stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid deriving comic effect from another's suffering, deformity, gross physical distress, or indecent gesture. Examples of anti-patterns: laughing at afflicted characters, ghost entrances, overblown battle/heroics, or other spectacles that appeal only to base appetites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable stage content: anything not contrary to virtue or good-manners
rubrics_metrics.description: I would not be understood in this Talk to argue, that nothing is tolerable on the Stage but what has an immediate Tendency to the Promotion of Virtue. On the contrary, I can allow, provided there is nothing against the Interests of Virtue, and is not offensive to Good-manners, that things of an indifferent nature may be represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights may include neutral or harmless amusements (rustic scenes, well-drawn comic touches) so long as they do not undermine virtue or offend decent manners. The essay praises particular comic performances (e.g., Dogget's Hob) while condemning material that panders to low tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors must not improvise lines that pander to fools
rubrics_metrics.description: The intolerable Folly and Confidence of Players putting in Words of their own, does in a great measure feed the absurd Taste of the Audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors inserting their own words or seeking applause by catering to the gross part of the audience corrupts public taste. Anti-pattern: players who 'prefer the Applause of Fools to that of the reasonable part of the Company.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim performances at the intelligent part of the audience, not the gross
rubrics_metrics.description: The gross of an Audience is composed of two sorts of People ... and those who improve or command corporeal Pleasures by the addition of fine Sentiments of the Mind. At present the intelligent part of the Company are wholly subdued, by the Insurrections of those who know no Satisfactions but what they have in common with all other Animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and actors should maintain standards that engage the thoughtful spectators rather than pandering to base appetites; the reception of a piece (applause, laughter) reveals audience disposition and should guide artistic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid spectacles that substitute noise or physical stunts for genuine comic subtlety
rubrics_metrics.description: To enumerate the entrance of Ghosts, the Embattling of Armies, the Noise of Heroes in Love, with a thousand other Enormities, would be to transgress the bounds of this Paper...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic or sensational stage devices (noisy battles, ghost-entrances, exaggerated heroics) often appeal to the wrong part of the audience and should not replace finely drawn comic situations or character-based humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of forms of wit (ranking and social valuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of this nature is the agreeable Pastime in Country-Halls of Cross-purposes, Questions and Commands... Then above them are such as can make Verses... Commend me also to those who have not Brains enough for any of these Exercises... That which we call Punning is therefore greatly affected by Men of small Intellects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different types of playful talk are socially ranked: parlor pastimes (cross-purposes, crambo) are low but serviceable; making verses is higher; punning is mechanical and associated with low intellect; double-entenders are coarse and appeal to the unbred. Writers/performers should prefer more substantial exercises of wit over mere punning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-meanings and immodest humour are signs of bad breeding
rubrics_metrics.description: There are another Kind of People of small Faculties, who supply want of Wit with want of Breeding; and because Women are both by Nature and Education more offended at any thing which is immodest than we Men are, these are ever harping upon things they ought not to allude to, and deal mightily in double Meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immodest or sexually double-meaning jokes cater to coarse tastes and should be avoided by an honest gentleman or a writer seeking refined amusement; such humour offends good manners and is favoured by the sillier part of society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and moral critique of 'Biting' (deceptive wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Biter is one who tells you a thing you have no reason to disbelieve in it self ... and if you give him Credit, laughs in your Face, and triumphs that he has deceiv'd you. In a Word, a Biter is one who thinks you a Fool, because you do not think him a Knave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biting is celebrated as an amusing device but morally condemned as a form of knavery that depends on deceiving the listener. The essay both praises its effectiveness as 'pleasant' and warns of its pernicious, frivolous character with concrete exemplars (the surgeon/condemned-man anecdote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Punning as a mechanical substitute for wit — anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Punning ... may be arrived at with the smallest Capacity ... Punning is therefore greatly affected by Men of small Intellects... they go on for ever, without Possibility of being exhausted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puns are described as mechanical, tiresome, and used by those lacking genuine imagination. Performers relying on puns are of low comic calibre; conversely, a man of wit should avoid relying chiefly on puns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public worship decorum: modesty and sobriety in church
rubrics_metrics.description: She might have stay'd at her own Parish, and not come to perplex those who are otherwise intent upon their Duty... I desire you would print this, that she may be confin'd to her own Parish; for I can assure you there is no attending any thing else in a Place where she is a Novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In places of worship, ostentatious dress, theatrical behaviour, or seeking personal admiration is improper because it distracts devotion. Social enforcement by fellow parishioners is implied ('keep these agreeable Disturbances out of the City').

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenting/family virtue: education and industry over mere inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: It is my Business to implant in every one of my Children the same Seeds of Industry, and the same honest Principles... I am persuaded ... That a Man who has many Children, and gives them a good Education, is more likely to raise a Family, than he who has but one, notwithstanding he leaves him his whole Estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good parenting consists in imparting industry and honest principles; quantity of children plus proper education is preferable to a single heir with an estate. This is presented as a practical maxim for producing successful offspring (examples: aspiring to have a general, admiral, etc., among one's children).
